a: and we took hold of him
t: "And wanted to judge him by our law" (24:6b)
p: The KJV continues Tertullus' speech here with words found in a minority of later manuscripts. This goes with 24:7 and 24:8.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74 (600s), Codex Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03) and the Byzantine majority as edited by Robinson and Pierpont
readings.plain: and we took hold of him

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV); Codex Laudianus (E, 500s), Ψ, minuscules 33, 614 and 1739 and some others, some Old Latin and Vulgate copies, the Syriac (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ὃν καὶ ἐκρατήσαμεν, καὶ κατὰ τὸν ἡμέτερον νόμον ἠθελήσαμεν κρίνειν
readings.en: whom we seized, and wanted to judge according to our law
readings.plain: and we took hold of him and wanted to judge him by our own law

why: The words are missing from the oldest manuscripts of every kind and from most later ones too, even the Byzantine majority. They look like an expansion that makes Tertullus' complaint clearer.
b: The longer text (24:6b–8a) has Tertullus say the Jews meant to try Paul themselves until Lysias took him away by force. It shifts blame onto the Roman commander and makes "him" in 24:8 refer to Lysias rather than Paul. Its wording is good Lukan Greek, and a few scholars think it original; most agree with Metzger that it was added.

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
p: The verse the KJV prints as 24:7 is found only in some later manuscripts. It goes with the additions at 24:6 and 24:8.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Codex Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03); the Byzantine majority (Robinson-Pierpont)
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV 24:7); Codex Laudianus (E, 500s), Ψ, minuscules 33, 614 and 1739 and others, some Old Latin and Vulgate copies, the Syriac (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: παρελθὼν δὲ Λυσίας ὁ χιλίαρχος μετὰ πολλῆς βίας ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ἡμῶν ἀπήγαγε
readings.en: but the commander Lysias came and with great violence took him away out of our hands
readings.plain: But Lysias the commander came along and took him out of our hands by great force.

why: The oldest manuscripts lack the verse, and so does the bulk of the Byzantine tradition; it reached the KJV through Erasmus' printed Greek, which followed later manuscripts that had it. This translation keeps the KJV numbering and marks the verse as absent.
b: With this verse, Tertullus accuses the Roman commander of interfering. The scene in 21:31–36 shows Lysias rescuing Paul from a mob, not from a court. The longer text may come from a reader who wanted to explain why the Jews had not tried Paul themselves.

t: "Commanding his accusers to come to you" (24:8a)
p: The KJV begins 24:8 with words that finish the added verse 24:7. This goes with 24:6 and 24:7.

readings.plain: He ordered his accusers to come before you. If you question him yourself

why: Part of the same addition as 24:6b and 24:7, missing from the oldest witnesses.
b: In the shorter text, "him" is Paul: Felix can question the prisoner. In the longer text, the nearest man named is Lysias, so Felix is invited to question the commander, which is what Felix then proposes to do (24:22).

p: The KJV says "a resurrection of the dead." The oldest manuscripts lack "of the dead."

why: The shorter reading has the oldest support; "of the dead" is the usual phrase and was easily added. The meaning does not change.

p: The KJV begins "And when Felix heard these things." The oldest manuscripts begin with Felix putting off the case.

why: The opening phrase is a natural link that copyists added to smooth the start of the sentence; the oldest manuscripts lack it. The meaning does not change.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add that his friends could also visit him.

Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "the faith in Christ"), Tregelles

readings.plain: hand him some money, so that he would let him go

why: The added clause explains what the bribe was for, which the context already makes plain. It is absent from the earliest witnesses.

a: the chief priests and the foremost men
p: The KJV has "the high priest." The oldest manuscripts have "the chief priests."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus
readings.en: the chief priests and the leading men
readings.plain: the chief priests and the foremost men

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: the high priest and the leading men
readings.plain: the high priest and the foremost men

why: "Chief priests" has the older support and matches 25:15. A scribe may have changed it to name the one high priest, as in 24:1.
b: By now Ananias was no longer high priest. Agrippa II had appointed Ishmael son of Phiabi (Josephus, Antiquities 20.179).

a: no more than eight or ten days
t: "Eight or ten days" or "more than ten days"
p: The KJV says Festus stayed "more than ten days." The oldest manuscripts say "not more than eight or ten."

readings.plain: no more than eight or ten days

why: The unusual "eight or ten" is better attested and harder; a copyist could easily simplify it to "more than ten."

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "to destruction": hand a man over to die.

readings.plain: making a gift of any man

p: The KJV has "And he said." The critical editions name the speaker: "the Lord said."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "And he said")

why: The oldest manuscripts name the speaker "the Lord," taking up Paul's question "Who are you, Lord?" The parallel accounts have no noun here (9:5; 22:8), which may be why copyists dropped it to match them. Either way the speaker is Jesus.

a: to what you have seen of me
p: Some manuscripts say Paul is a witness to the things in which he has "seen me"; others just "seen."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (in brackets), Tyndale House; Vaticanus and other manuscripts
readings.en: of the things in which you saw me
readings.plain: to what you have seen of me

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "of these things which thou hast seen"); P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus

why: The manuscripts are closely divided, and NA28 prints "me" in brackets. "Seen me" matches "I will appear to you" in the same sentence, which may be why it was kept, or why it was added.

p: The oldest manuscripts say "to make (or play) a Christian"; the Byzantine text has the easier "to become a Christian."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus
readings.en: you persuade me to make (myself) a Christian

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "to be a Christian")
readings.en: you persuade me to become a Christian

why: "Make" is the harder reading and has the oldest witnesses; "become" smooths the Greek. Codex Alexandrinus has a slightly different verb, πείθῃ, "you are confident" (reported by Metzger).
b: "Make a Christian" may mean "make me a Christian" or "act the part of a Christian." On "almost" in the KJV, see the note on "With so little."

p: The KJV begins "And when he had thus spoken." The oldest manuscripts begin with the king rising.

Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "And when he had thus spoken, the king rose up")

readings.en: and when he had said these things, the king rose
readings.plain: When he had said this, the king stood up

why: A linking phrase that copyists added to mark the end of Paul's speech; the oldest witnesses lack it. The meaning does not change.

a: It was about to call at towns
t: The ship or "we" about to sail
p: In the oldest manuscripts the ship is about to sail along Asia. In the KJV it is "we" who mean to sail.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus

readings.plain: It was about to call at towns

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia")
readings.orig: πλοίῳ Ἀδραμυττηνῷ, μέλλοντες πλεῖν τοὺς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν τόπους
readings.en: an Adramyttian ship, we intending to sail the places along Asia
readings.plain: We meant to call at towns

why: The difference is a single ending: the ship "about to" sail, or "we" about to sail. The critical editions make the ship the subject. The route is the same either way.

p: A few Western witnesses add that the crossing to Myra took fifteen days.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus; all the major manuscripts
Minuscule 614 and a few others, and the Harclean Syriac marked with an asterisk (reported by Metzger)
readings.plain: Over fifteen days we crossed the waters

why: Only a few Western witnesses have it. It may preserve a real detail, but it is more likely a scribe's addition.

p: The KJV calls the storm "Euroclydon." The oldest manuscripts have "Euraquilo," the northeaster.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus; the Latin Vulgate (euroaquilo)
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Euroclydon")

why: "Euraquilo" is a sailors' hybrid of Greek Euros (east wind) and Latin Aquilo (north wind), the east-northeaster. It is the stranger word and has the oldest witnesses. Copyists who did not know it seem to have turned it into Euroclydon, "east wind that stirs up waves."
b: A Latin wind-rose cut in a pavement at Thugga (modern Dougga, Tunisia) names the winds of the compass, and one of them is this same Greek-Latin hybrid for the east-northeast wind. Hemer cites it as evidence that sailors really used the name; the Latin Vulgate also has euroaquilo.

p: The KJV has "Clauda." Manuscripts spell the island's name three ways. Today it is Gavdos.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; P74, Vaticanus and others (reported by Metzger)
Tyndale House; Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Alexandrinus and others (reported by Metzger)
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Clauda")

why: All three spellings name the same island, and both Cauda and Clauda were in use in antiquity. SBL and NA28 prefer Cauda, which agrees with the Gaudos that Pliny the Elder already uses (Natural History 4.61) and with today's Gavdos. Tyndale House prefers Clauda, which has Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus behind it.

p: The KJV says "we cast out" the tackle. The oldest manuscripts say "they."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "we cast out")

why: "They" has the older witnesses. "We" may be a copyist's attempt to make the passengers share the work, as in 27:16.

p: Codex Vaticanus says "about seventy-six." The difference may come from how the numbers were written.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus; Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and nearly all others
Westcott-Hort; Codex Vaticanus (03, 300s) and the Sahidic Coptic (reported by Metzger)

why: Nearly all witnesses read 276. In Greek numerals 276 was ΣΟϚ and "about" was ΩΣ; written together as ΩΣΣΟϚ, the doubled S could easily be dropped or added. Most editors think 276 is original (Westcott and Hort, who often followed Vaticanus, printed "about seventy-six") and the large number fits a grain ship (Josephus' ship had about 600).

a: by the force of the waves
p: The SBLGNT, following two great manuscripts, has only "by the force." NA28 and Tyndale House include "of the waves."

readings.w: NA28 (in brackets), Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "by the violence of the waves"); Alexandrinus and most manuscripts
readings.en: by the force of the waves
readings.plain: by the force of the waves

readings.w: SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort; Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus (reported by Metzger)

why: Here the Plain follows NA28 and Tyndale House against the SBLGNT. "Of the waves" is widely attested, and without it the Greek is abrupt. But it could also be a natural addition to explain "the force," which is why NA28 brackets it. The sense is the same either way.

p: The KJV has "they knew." The oldest manuscripts keep the "we" of the narrator.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "then they knew")

why: The first person has the older support and fits the "we" narrative that runs through 28:16.

p: The editions differ by one letter: "having cast off" or "having gone around" (KJV "fetched a compass").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort; Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus (reported by Metzger)
Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "we fetched a compass"); P74, Alexandrinus and most manuscripts

why: The two words differ only by θ. "Cast off" uses the same verb as 27:40 ("cut away the anchors") and is the harder reading; "sailed around" is the easier word copyists would expect. Tyndale House prefers the majority reading, so the choice is close. The route is the same either way.

p: The KJV says the centurion handed the prisoners to "the captain of the guard." The oldest manuscripts lack it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus; the Vulgate

Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard: but Paul was suffered"); minuscule 614, the Harclean Syriac, the Old Latin (gig), with Western variations
readings.orig: ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος παρέδωκεν τοὺς δεσμίους τῷ στρατοπεδάρχῃ, τῷ δὲ Παύλῳ ἐπετράπη
readings.en: the centurion handed over the prisoners to the camp commander, but Paul was permitted
readings.plain: the centurion handed the prisoners over to the camp commander, but Paul was given permission

why: The sentence is absent from the oldest witnesses and looks like a Western expansion that explains what happened to the other prisoners. Some Old Latin copies add that Paul was allowed to stay "outside the camp."
b: Who was the stratopedarchēs, "camp commander"? Suggestions include the prefect of the Praetorian Guard (in 60–62, Afranius Burrus), the officer in charge of the Praetorian camp, or the commander of the frumentarii, officers who handled couriers and prisoners. The detail may preserve good local knowledge even if it was added.

a: But the Jews spoke against it
p: A few Western witnesses add that the Jews shouted, "Away with our enemy!"

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus; all the major manuscripts
readings.plain: But the Jews spoke against it

readings.w: Minuscule 614 and a few others, and the Harclean Syriac marked with an asterisk (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ἀντιλεγόντων δὲ τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ ἐπικραζόντων· Αἶρε τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἡμῶν
readings.en: but when the Jews objected and cried out, 'Away with our enemy!'
readings.plain: But the Jews spoke against it and cried out, 'Away with our enemy!'

why: Found in only a few late witnesses. It echoes the cries against Jesus (Luke 23:18) and against Paul (21:36; 22:22), and is best explained as a scribe's dramatic addition.

p: The KJV has "our fathers." The oldest manuscripts have "your fathers."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "unto our fathers")

why: "Your" has the oldest support. In Greek of this period ὑμῶν and ἡμῶν sounded alike, so the change is easy. "Your" puts a little distance between Paul and those who refuse, as Stephen's speech did (7:51–52); "our" keeps him one of them, as in 28:17.

p: The verse the KJV prints as 28:29 is missing from the oldest manuscripts.

readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
